s: desert crossing lasts twelve days and nights (while carrying Argo)
q: and bare her twelve days and nights alike.

s: Poseidon is considered father of Triton
q: For my sire Poseidon has made me to be well versed in this sea.

s: Amphitrite loosens Poseidon (straightway)
q: when Amphitrite has straightway loosed Poseidon’s swift-wheeled car

s: Ladon guards golden apples (in the garden of Atlas)
q: where Ladon, the serpent of the land, till yesterday kept watch over the golden apples in the garden of Atlas

s: Hesperides is a nymphs
q: and all around the nymphs, the Hesperides, were busied, chanting their lovely song.

s: Hesperides lament shrilly
q: And close at hand the Hesperides, their white arms flung over their golden heads, lamented shrilly

s: Orpheus marks the divine portent
q: Orpheus marked the divine portent, and for his comrades addressed them in prayer

s: Orpheus orders bringing Apollo’s massy tripod (from the ship)
q: Then straightway Orpheus bade them bring forth from the ship Apollo’s massy tripod and offer it to the gods of the land as propitiation for their return.

s: Caphaurus is a shepherd (defending his sheep)
q: for he was no weakling, Caphaurus, the grandson of Lycoreian Phoebus and the chaste maiden Acacallis

s: Caphaurus is grandson of Phoebus
q: Caphaurus, the grandson of Lycoreian Phoebus and the chaste maiden Acacallis

s: Caphaurus is grandson of Acacallis
q: Caphaurus, the grandson of Lycoreian Phoebus and the chaste maiden Acacallis

s: Canthus is killed by a shepherd (by the cast of a stone)
q: and there followed a shepherd who, in defence of his own sheep, while thou weft leading them off[37] to thy comrades in their need, slew thee by the cast of a stone

s: death of Canthus occurs in Libya
q: But thee, Canthus, the fates of death seized in Libya.

s: north wind drives Argo (in mid-course)
q: even then a baleful blast of the north wind seized them in mid-course and swept them towards the Libyan sea nine nights and as many days

s: Mopsus is a son of Ampycus
q: Thereupon on the same day a pitiless fate seized Mopsus too, son of Ampycus

s: death of Mopsus is bitten by it (between the shin and the muscles)
q: Mopsus stepped on the end of its spine, setting thereon the sole of his left foot; and it writhed round in pain and bit and tore the flesh between the shin and the muscles.

s: burial rites are performed for Mopsus (by the Argonauts)
q: And quickly and in haste they dug a deep grave with mattocks of bronze; and they tore their hair, the heroes and the maidens, bewailing the dead man’s piteous suffering; and when he had received due burial rites, thrice they marched round the tomb in full armour, and heaped above him a mound of earth.

s: tripod of Apollo is offered to the gods of the land (as propitiation for their return)
q: Then straightway Orpheus bade them bring forth from the ship Apollo’s massy tripod and offer it to the gods of the land as propitiation for their return.

s: Triton has sire Poseidon
q: For my sire Poseidon has made me to be well versed in this sea. And I rule the shore if haply in your distant land you have ever heard of Eurypylus, born in Libya, the home of wild beasts.

s: Triton is also called Phoreys (as a sea god)
q: Thou god, who hast manifested thyself on the borders of this land, whether the daughters born of the sea call thee Triton, the great sea-marvel, or Phoreys, or Nereus

s: Triton is also called Nereus (as a sea god)
q: Thou god, who hast manifested thyself on the borders of this land, whether the daughters born of the sea call thee Triton, the great sea-marvel, or Phoreys, or Nereus

s: Triton guides Argo (from the Tritonian lake into the sea)
q: And as when a man trains a swift steed for the broad race-course, and runs along, grasping the bushy mane, while the steed follows obeying his master, and rears his neck aloft in his pride, and the gleaming bit rings loud as he champs it in his jaws from side to side; so the god, seizing hollow Argo’s keel, guided her onward to the sea.

s: Libyan sea contains Syrtis (far within it)
q: until they came far within Syrtis, wherefrom is no return for ships, when they are once forced into that gulf.

s: Argonauts’ return voyage is desired by Minyae (to Achaea)
q: with these words: “Thou god, who hast manifested thyself on the borders of this land, whether the daughters born of the sea call thee Triton, the great sea-marvel, or Phoreys, or Nereus, be gracious, and grant the return home dear to our hearts

s: Syrtis has shoals (on every hand)
q: For on every hand are shoals, on every hand masses of seaweed from the depths

s: Syrtis has stretch of sand (to the dim horizon)
q: and there is a stretch of sand to the dim horizon

s: flood-tide drives Argo (onto the innermost shore)
q: Here accordingly the flood-tide—for this tide often retreats from the land and bursts back again over the beach coming on with a rush and roar—thrust them suddenly on to the innermost shore

s: Argo is a ship
q: And miserably long ago would our sacred ship have been shattered far from the shore; but the tide itself bore her high on to the land from the deep sea.

s: Argo has harbour the harbour of Argo
q: There is the harbour of Argo and there are the signs of her stay, and altars to Poseidon and Triton; for during that day they tarried.

s: Talos is last survivor of men sprung from ash-trees (among the sons of the gods)
q: He was of the stock of bronze, of the men sprung from ash-trees, the last left among the sons of the gods

s: Talos is a son of the gods (the last left among them)
q: He was of the stock of bronze, of the men sprung from ash-trees, the last left among the sons of the gods

s: Talos has body bronze (throughout most of his body and limbs)
q: Now in all the rest of his body and limbs was he fashioned of bronze and invulnerable

s: Talos is invulnerable bronze body and limbs (except at the ankle vein)
q: Now in all the rest of his body and limbs was he fashioned of bronze and invulnerable

s: Talos has life vein Talos’s life-vein (beneath the sinew by his ankle)
q: but beneath the sinew by his ankle was a blood-red vein; and this, with its issues of life and death, was covered by a thin skin.

s: Talos’s life-vein controls the death of Talos (with its issues of life and death)
q: but beneath the sinew by his ankle was a blood-red vein; and this, with its issues of life and death, was covered by a thin skin.

s: Talos is warder of Crete (striding round the island thrice a day)
q: and the son of Cronos gave him to Europa to be the warder of Crete and to stride round the island thrice a day with his feet of bronze.

s: Cronos is father of Zeus (the son of Cronos)
q: and the son of Cronos gave him to Europa to be the warder of Crete

s: Europa has received Talos (as warder of Crete)
q: and the son of Cronos gave him to Europa to be the warder of Crete

s: Argo has altars to Poseidon (at her harbour)
q: There is the harbour of Argo and there are the signs of her stay, and altars to Poseidon and Triton; for during that day they tarried.

s: Medea is a sorceress
q: So Talos, for all his frame of bronze, yielded the victory to the might of Medea the sorceress.

s: Medea can subdue Talos (by sorcery)
q: For I deem that I alone can subdue for you that man, whoever he be, even though his frame be of bronze throughout

s: Medea invokes Death-spirits (as devourers of life and swift hounds of Hades)
q: And with songs did she propitiate and invoke the Death-spirits, devourers of life, the swift hounds of Hades

s: Jason is a son of Aeson
q: and Aeson’s son took her hand in his and guided her way along the thwarts.

s: Athena has shrine shrine (built by the Argonauts in Crete)
q: they built a shrine to Minoan Athena

s: Pall of Darkness is a night (fatal and without stars, moonlight, or heavenly beams)
q: night scared them, that night which they name the Pall of Darkness; the stars pierced not that fatal night nor the beams of the moon

s: Phoebus is a Apollo (called the Gleamer)
q: and they made for Apollo a glorious abode in a shady wood, and a shady altar, calling on Phoebus the “Gleamer”

s: Phoebus reveals Anaphe (to men sore bewildered)
q: and that bare island they called Anaphe,[39] for that Phoebus had revealed it to men sore bewildered

s: Argo has altars to Triton (at her harbour)
q: There is the harbour of Argo and there are the signs of her stay, and altars to Poseidon and Triton; for during that day they tarried.

s: Anaphe is named for Phoebus (because he revealed it to the bewildered men)
q: and that bare island they called Anaphe,[39] for that Phoebus had revealed it to men sore bewildered

s: Medea’s Phaeacian handmaids has seen Phaeacians (in the halls of Alcinous)
q: for that ever they had seen oxen in plenty slain in the halls of Alcinous.

s: Libya is parent of Euphemus’s dream-woman (through Triton)
q: Daughter of Triton am I, dear friend, and nurse of thy children, no maiden; Triton and Libya are my parents.

s: Calliste is a island (created from the clod cast into the sea)
q: Therefrom rose up an island, Calliste, sacred nurse of the sons of Euphemus

s: Calliste is sacred nurse of Euphemus (for his sons)
q: Therefrom rose up an island, Calliste, sacred nurse of the sons of Euphemus

s: Aegina is a island (a beach where the Argonauts stopped)
q: And thence they steadily left behind long leagues of sea and stayed on the beach of Aegina

s: Argonauts is a heroes
q: So the heroes, though outworn with toil, quickly backed their ship from the land in sore dismay.

s: Pagasae is a beach (where the Argonauts came ashore)
q: and gladly did ye step forth upon the beach of Pagasae.

s: Crete is a island (rising in the sea above other islands)
q: and thence they were to cross to Crete, which rises in the sea above other islands.

s: Crete has warder Talos (appointed by Zeus for the island)
q: and the son of Cronos gave him to Europa to be the warder of Crete

s: Crete contains Dicte’s haven
q: when they came to the roadstead of Dicte’s haven.

s: Talos is a man of bronze
q: And Talos, the man of bronze, as he broke off rocks from the hard cliff, stayed them from fastening hawsers to the shore

s: Talos is from men sprung from ash-trees (of their stock)
q: He was of the stock of bronze, of the men sprung from ash-trees, the last left among the sons of the gods

s: Argus is a shipwright (son of Arestor and helper of Athena)
q: and with her Argus, son of Arestor, wrought it by her counsels.

s: Argus is related to Athena (works under her guidance)
q: The ship, as former bards relate, Argus wrought by the guidance of Athena.

s: Athena is a goddess (Tritonian)
q: Tritonian Athena herself urged him to join the band of chiefs

s: Athena fashions Argo (with Argus’s assistance)
q: She herself too fashioned the swift ship; and with her Argus, son of Arestor, wrought it by her counsels.

s: golden fleece is a quest object
q: sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.

s: Pontus is a sea (crossed by the Argonauts)
q: down through the mouth of Pontus and between the Cyanean rocks

s: Cyanean rocks is a rocks (lying in the route of the voyage)
q: down through the mouth of Pontus and between the Cyanean rocks

s: Poseidon is honoured by Pelias (at a banquet)
q: the banquet which the king was offering to his father Poseidon and the rest of the gods

s: Pelias neglects Pelasgian Hera (at his banquet)
q: though he paid no honour to Pelasgian Hera.

s: Jason is a son of Alcimede
q: thus Jason himself was the son of Alcimede who was born of Clymene the daughter of Minyas.

s: Orpheus is a son of Calliope (according to report)
q: First then let us name Orpheus whom once Calliope bare, it is said, wedded to Thracian Oeagrus

s: Orpheus is a musician (his songs possess magical power)
q: Men say that he by the music of his songs charmed the stubborn rocks upon the mountains and the course of rivers.

s: Polyphemus is a son of Eilatus
q: Next to them from Larisa came Polyphemus, son of Eilatus

s: Polyphemus fought against Centaurs (in his younger days)
q: when they were arming themselves against the Centaurs, fought in his younger days

s: Jason undertakes golden fleece quest (at Pelias’s behest)
q: who, at the behest of King Pelias, down through the mouth of Pontus and between the Cyanean rocks, sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.

s: Alcimede is a daughter of Phylacus (wife of Aeson)
q: for Aeson had wedded his sister Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus

s: Mopsus is a seer (taught augury by Leto’s son)
q: There came too Titaresian Mopsus, whom above all men the son of Leto taught the augury of birds

s: Jason has helpers the helpers
q: So many then were the helpers who assembled to join the son of Aeson.

s: Canthus is fated to die in Libya (he is not destined to return to Cerinthus)
q: but he was not destined to return to Cerinthus. For fate had ordained that he and Mopsus, skilled in the seer’s art, should wander and perish in the furthest ends of Libya.

s: Peleus is a son of Aeacus (made his home in Phthia)
q: Telamon dwelt in the Attic island; but Peleus departed and made his home in Phthia.

s: Tiphys is a son of Hagnias (skilled in seafaring and weather prediction)
q: Tiphys, son of Hagnias, left the Siphaean people of the Thespians, well skilled to foretell the rising wave on the broad sea, and well skilled to infer from sun and star the stormy winds and the time for sailing.

s: Heracles has mighty heart mighty heart
q: Nor do we learn that Heracles of the mighty heart disregarded the eager summons of Aeson’s son.

s: Heracles is related to Hylas (Hylas is his young companion and arms-bearer)
q: and with him went Hylas, a brave comrade, in the flower of youth, to bear his arrows and to guard his bow.

s: Pelias receives Pelias’s oracle (concerning his death)
q: Such was the oracle that Pelias heard, that a hateful doom awaited him to be slain at the prompting of the man whom he should see coming forth from the people with but one sandal.

s: Heracles opposes Eurystheus (acts against Eurystheus’s purpose)
q: and himself of his own will set out against the purpose of Eurystheus

s: Hylas is a companion of Heracles (young and brave; bears his arrows and guards his bow)
q: and with him went Hylas, a brave comrade, in the flower of youth, to bear his arrows and to guard his bow.

s: Idmon is a seer (son of Apollo but publicly counted as son of Abas)
q: He was not in truth the son of Abas, but Leto’s son himself begat him to be numbered among the illustrious Aeolids; and himself taught him the art of prophecy

s: Idmon knows his own fate (through augury)
q: for though he had learnt his own fate by augury, he came, that the people might not grudge him fair renown.

s: Polydeuces is a son of Leda (strong; skilled to guide swift-footed steeds)
q: Moreover Aetolian Leda sent from Sparta strong Polydeuces and Castor, skilled to guide swift-footed steeds

s: Pelias is a king
q: who, at the behest of King Pelias, down through the mouth of Pontus and between the Cyanean rocks, sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.

s: Idas is a son of Aphareus (exulting in great strength)
q: The sons of Aphareus, Lynceus and proud Idas, came from Arene, both exulting in their great strength

s: Augeias desires to see Aeetes (in Colchis)
q: and greatly he desired to behold the Colchian land and Aeetes himself the ruler of the Colchians.

s: Aeetes is a ruler of Colchis (Colchian king)
q: Aeetes himself the ruler of the Colchians.

s: Euphemus skims the swell of the grey sea (without wetting his swift feet)
q: He was wont to skim the swell of the grey sea, and wetted not his swift feet, but just dipping the tips of his toes was borne on the watery path.

s: Argo is a ship (swift and excellent)
q: She herself too fashioned the swift ship; and with her Argus, son of Arestor, wrought it by her counsels. Wherefore it proved the most excellent of all ships that have made trial of the sea with oars.

s: Zetes is a son of Boreas (winged)
q: Next came Zetes and Calais, sons of Boreas

s: Calais is a son of Boreas (winged)
q: Next came Zetes and Calais, sons of Boreas

s: Minyae is a Argonauts (the name used for the assembled heroes)
q: All the chiefs the dwellers thereabout called Minyae

s: Minyae are descended from daughters of Minyas (most and bravest claimed this descent)
q: for the most and the bravest avowed that they were sprung from the blood of the daughters of Minyas

s: Argonaut gathering is a assembly of heroes (formed to join Jason)
q: So many then were the helpers who assembled to join the son of Aeson.

s: Pelias’s oracle foretells Pelias’s death (at the hands of the one-sandaled man)
q: Such was the oracle that Pelias heard, that a hateful doom awaited him to be slain at the prompting of the man whom he should see coming forth from the people with but one sandal.

s: Argo is used for golden fleece quest
q: sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.

s: golden fleece quest undertaken by Argo (in quest of the golden fleece)
q: sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.

s: Alcimede is a Achaean woman (once admired among the women)
q: Now I, once so admired among Achaean women, shall be left behind like a bondwoman in my empty halls

s: Aeson is father of Jason
q: Aeson too, ill-fated man! Surely better had it been for him, if he were lying beneath the earth

s: Minyan heroes is a heroes (half-divine and exceptionally brave)
q: On that day all the gods looked down from heaven upon the ship and the might of the heroes, half-divine, the bravest of men then sailing the sea

s: Minyan heroes constitute Argonauts (the expedition's crew)
q: And the heroes went to the benches one after the other, as they had previously assigned for each to row in his place

s: Heracles is a hero (regarded as the bravest candidate for leadership)
q: Thus he spake; and the young heroes turned their eyes towards bold Heracles sitting in their midst, and with one shout they all enjoined upon him to be their leader

s: Heracles declines leadership (in favor of Jason)
q: Let no one offer this honour to me. For I will not consent, and I will forbid any other to stand up. Let the hero who brought us together, himself be the leader of the host.”

s: Heracles occupies the middle bench (with Ancaeus)
q: but the middle bench they chose for Heracles and Ancaeus apart from the other heroes

s: Tiphys is a helmsman (of Argos)
q: with one consent they entrusted Tiphys with guarding the helm of the well-stemmed ship

s: Jason is son of Aeson
q: And Aeson’s son poured out pure libations

s: Ancaeus occupies the middle bench (with Heracles)
q: but the middle bench they chose for Heracles and Ancaeus apart from the other heroes

s: Idmon foresees Argonauts’ return voyage (for the heroes)
q: For you it is the will of heaven and destiny that ye shall return here with the fleece

s: Idmon’s prophecy foretells Idmon’s death (somewhere on the mainland of Asia)
q: but meanwhile both going and returning, countless trials await you. But it is my lot, by the hateful decree of a god, to die somewhere afar off on the mainland of Asia.

s: Orpheus is a singer (playing the lyre)
q: and Orpheus lifted his lyre in his left hand and made essay to sing.

s: Zeus dwells in the Dictaean cave (still a child)
q: while Zeus, still a child and with the thoughts of a child, dwelt in the Dictaean cave

s: Apollo promises Jason (to show the paths of the sea)
q: thou who didst promise me, when I sought thy oracle at Pytho, to show the fulfilment and goal of my journey

s: Athena provides the divine beam of Argo (from the oak of Dodona)
q: For in her a beam divine had been laid which Athena had brought from an oak of Dodona and fitted in the middle of the stem.

s: Argo is a ship (called Pelian Argo)
q: And a strange cry did the harbour of Pagasae utter, yea and Pelian Argo herself, urging them to set forth.

s: Argo contains the divine beam of Argo (fitted in the middle of the stem)
q: For in her a beam divine had been laid which Athena had brought from an oak of Dodona and fitted in the middle of the stem.

s: Argo is guided by Tiphys (at the helm)
q: Now when they had left the curving shore of the harbour through the cunning and counsel of prudent Tiphys son of Hagnias, who skilfully handled the well-polished helm that he might guide them steadfastly

s: Apollo of the Dawn is a epithet of Apollo (invoked as guide of embarkation)
q: Meantime let us build upon the beach an altar to Apollo Embasius[5] who by an oracle promised to point out and show me the paths of the sea

s: the oracle of Apollo promises Jason (guidance on the sea voyage)
q: who by an oracle promised to point out and show me the paths of the sea

s: the sacrifice to Apollo is offered at the altar to Apollo (before embarkation)
q: And now, come, Far-darter, accept this sacrifice at our hands, which first of all we have offered thee for this ship on our embarcation

s: Pagasae contains the beach of Pagasae (where Argos lies on the strand)
q: then the heroes took their way through the city to the ship where it lay on the strand that men call Magnesian Pagasae

s: Mount Pelion has nymphs the nymphs of Pelion (on the topmost heights)
q: and on the topmost heights the nymphs of Pelion wondered as they beheld the work of Itonian Athena

s: Lemnos is a island (called the Sintian isle)
q: they reached Lemnos, the Sintian isle.

s: the Argonauts’ departure from Iolcos is accompanied by many thralls, men and women (at the departure of the heroes)
q: Thus the women spake at the departure of the heroes. And now many thralls, men and women, were gathered together, and his mother, smitten with grief for Jason.

s: the launch of Argo occurs in the sea
q: she glided into the sea; but the heroes stood there and kept dragging her back as she sped onward

s: Jason receives guidance from the oracle of Apollo (for the venture)
q: for very favourable oracles has Phoebus given

s: Alcimede is mother of Jason (grieving at his departure)
q: And even as the mother had thrown her arms about her son, so she clung, weeping without stint

s: Lemnian men are slain in the Lemnian massacre (all males of the people except Thoas)
q: Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly slain through the transgressions of the women in the year gone by.

s: Hypsipyle sends Thoas’s chest (with Thoas inside it to escape by sea)
q: and she sent him in a hollow chest, to drift over the sea, if haply he should escape.

s: Thoas is a king (of the Lemnian people before the massacre)
q: And of all the women, Hypsipyle alone spared her aged father Thoas, who was king over the people;

s: Thoas is father of Hypsipyle
q: and with them Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, donned her father’s harness.

s: Thoas escapes in Thoas’s chest (after being spared by Hypsipyle)
q: and she sent him in a hollow chest, to drift over the sea, if haply he should escape.

s: Lemnian women hold the Lemnian women’s assembly (at Hypsipyle’s command)
q: Now the Lemnian women fared through the city and sat down to the assembly, for Hypsipyle herself had so bidden.

s: the Lemnian women’s assembly is led by Hypsipyle
q: Now the Lemnian women fared through the city and sat down to the assembly, for Hypsipyle herself had so bidden.

s: Polyxo advocates the Lemnian women’s alliance with the Argonauts (as a means of preserving the women and their city)
q: But I bid you who are younger give good heed to this. For now at your feet a way of escape lies open, if ye trust to the strangers the care of your homes and all your stock and your glorious city.

s: Iphinoe is messenger of Hypsipyle (to the Minyae)
q: She spake and addressed Iphinoe close at hand: “Go, Iphinoe, and beg yonder man, whoever it is that leads this array, to come to our land

s: Minyae are invited by Lemnian women (to enter Lemnos peacefully)
q: and she bids yourselves, if ye wish it, straightway enter the land and the city with friendly intent.”

s: Lemnian men reject their lawful wives (in favor of captive maids)
q: For the men had rejected their lawful wives, loathing them, and had conceived a fierce passion for captive maids whom they themselves brought across the sea from their forays in Thrace;

s: Jason is sent on his way (by the Minyae)
q: And they deemed that Thoas was dead and that his beloved daughter Hypsipyle was queen, and quickly they sent Jason on his way and themselves made ready to go.

s: Jason possesses Jason’s purple mantle (a gift of Athena)
q: Now he had buckled round his shoulders a purple mantle of double fold, the work of the Tritonian goddess, which Pallas had given him

s: Jason possesses Jason’s spear (a gift from Atalanta)
q: And in his right hand Jason held a fardarting spear, which Atalanta gave him once as a gift of hospitality in Maenalus

s: Jason receives Hypsipyle’s offer of sovereignty (but declines it because of his quest)
q: But let the sovereignty of the island be thine; it is not in scorn I yield it up, but grievous trials urge me on.

s: Heracles opposes the Lemnian women’s alliance with the Argonauts (because it delays the fleece quest)
q: No fair renown shall we win by thus tarrying so long with stranger women; nor will some god seize and give us at our prayer a fleece that moves of itself.

s: Heracles urges Argonauts’ return voyage (to resume without delay)
q: Let us then return each to his own; but him leave ye to rest all day long in the embrace of Hypsipyle until he has peopled Lemnos with men-children, and so there come to him great glory.”

s: Argonauts’ return voyage is for golden fleece quest (to obtain the golden fleece)
q: Go, and may heaven bring thee back again with thy comrades unharmed, bearing to the king the golden fleece, even as thou wilt and thy heart desireth;

s: golden fleece is object of golden fleece quest
q: Go, and may heaven bring thee back again with thy comrades unharmed, bearing to the king the golden fleece, even as thou wilt and thy heart desireth;

s: Lemnian women are responsible for the Lemnian massacre (because of the marriage-bed conflict)
q: Not their husbands alone with the captives did they slay on account of the marriage-bed, but all the males at the same time, that they might thereafter pay no retribution for the grim murder.

s: Cypris is propitiated by Lemnian women (with songs and sacrifices)
q: and above all the immortals they propitiated with songs and sacrifices the illustrious son of Hera and Cypris herself.

s: Lemnos is a island (in the Aegean Sea)
q: and I deem that thou wilt not scorn our land at all; for it is deepsoiled beyond all other islands that lie in the Aegaean sea.

s: Lemnos is intended to be reinhabited by men (through the alliance with the Argonauts)
q: in order that Lemnos might be again inhabited by men and not be ruined.

s: Argonauts’ return voyage reaches the Hellespont (after passing the Rhoeteian shore, Ida, Dardania, Abydus, Percote, Abarnis, and Pityeia)
q: And in that night, as the ship sped on by sail and oar, they passed right through the Hellespont dark-gleaming with eddies

s: Argo is a ship (rowed and sailed by the Minyae)
q: So when they saw Argo being rowed near the island

s: Lemnian women kill Lemnian men (including husbands and captive maids’ partners)
q: Not their husbands alone with the captives did they slay on account of the marriage-bed, but all the males at the same time, that they might thereafter pay no retribution for the grim murder.

s: Lemnian women are capable of warfare (after taking up the men’s occupations)
q: Yet for all that did they often gaze over the broad sea, in grievous fear against the Thracians’ coming. So when they saw Argo being rowed near the island, straightway crowding in multitude from the gates of Myrine and clad in their harness of war

s: Lemnian women perform agriculture and cattle-tending (in place of the slain men)
q: Now for all the women to tend kine, to don armour of bronze, and to cleave with the plough-share the wheat-bearing fields, was easier than the works of Athena, with which they were busied aforetime.

s: Hypsipyle is a queen (of Lemnos)
q: And they deemed that Thoas was dead and that his beloved daughter Hypsipyle was queen

s: Hypsipyle is daughter of Thoas
q: and with them Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, donned her father’s harness.

s: Hypsipyle spares Thoas (during the Lemnian massacre)
q: And of all the women, Hypsipyle alone spared her aged father Thoas, who was king over the people;

s: Propontis contains a lofty island (a short distance from the Phrygian mainland)
q: There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the Phrygian mainland

s: Cyzicus son of Aeneus is a king (king of the Doliones)
q: over them Cyzicus son of Aeneus was king

s: Cyzicus son of Aeneus is born to Aenete (as her son)
q: whom Aenete the daughter of goodly Eusorus bare.

s: Argo is driven by the winds of Thrace
q: Thither Argo pressed on, driven by the winds of Thrace

s: Argo is driven by Thrace (by the winds of Thrace)
q: Thither Argo pressed on, driven by the winds of Thrace

s: Argo is received by Fair haven (as she reached it)
q: and the Fair haven received her as she sped.

s: Tiphys advises use of small anchorstone (as the first anchor)
q: There they cast away their small anchorstone by the advice of Tiphys

s: Doliones welcomes Argonauts (with friendliness and hospitality)
q: Now the Doliones and Cyzicus himself all came together to meet them with friendliness, and when they knew of the quest and their lineage welcomed them with hospitality

s: Cyzicus son of Aeneus welcomes Argonauts (with hospitality)
q: Now the Doliones and Cyzicus himself all came together to meet them with friendliness, and when they knew of the quest and their lineage welcomed them with hospitality

s: Cyzicus son of Aeneus is married to Cleite (his young bride)
q: his wife was untouched by the pangs of child-birth, the daughter of Percosian Merops, fair-haired Cleite

s: Dindymum has path of Jason (the route climbed by the heroes)
q: and the path they trod is named the path of Jason.

s: Earthborn attacks Argonauts (from the mountain above Chytus)
q: But the Earthborn men on the other side rushed down from the mountain and with crags below blocked up the mouth of vast Chytus towards the sea

s: Hera nurtures Earthborn (to make them a trial for Heracles)
q: For these dread monsters too, I ween, the goddess Hera, bride of Zeus, had nurtured to be a trial for Heracles.

s: Heracles kills Earthborn (during the battle at Chytus)
q: But there Heracles had been left behind with the younger heroes and he quickly bent his back-springing bow against the monsters and brought them to earth one after another

s: Cyzicus’s death is caused by Jason (in the mistaken night battle)
q: But Aeson’s son leapt upon him as he turned to face him, and smote him in the middle of the breast, and the bone was shattered round the spear

s: Cleite’s suicide is caused by Cyzicus’s death (after her husband’s death)
q: No, nor was his bride Cleite left behind her dead husband, but to crown the ill she wrought an ill yet more awful, when she clasped a noose round her neck

s: Cleite fountain is created from Cleite’s suicide (by the tears of the grove nymphs)
q: Her death even the nymphs of the grove bewailed; and of all the tears for her that they shed to earth from their eyes the goddesses made a fountain, which they call Cleite

s: twelve-day storm keeps Argonauts (from sailing)
q: After this, fierce tempests arose for twelve days and nights together and kept them there from sailing.

s: Mopsus is a seer (a prophetic interpreter)
q: the seer touched Jason as he lay wrapped in soft sheepskins and woke him at once

s: Mopsus interprets halcyon (as a good omen)
q: Mopsus heard and understood the cry of the bird of the shore, fraught with good omen.

s: Mother of the gods is a goddess (universal divine mother)
q: thou must climb to this temple on rugged Dindymum and propitiate the mother[13] of all the blessed gods

s: Mother of the gods controls winds (through her divine power)
q: For by her power the winds and the sea and all the earth below and the snowy seat of Olympus are complete

s: Rhea is invoked as mother of Dindymum (most venerable, dweller in Phrygia)
q: invoking the mother of Dindymum, most venerable, dweller in Phrygia

s: sacrifice to Rhea responds to pious sacrifices (favourable signs appeared)
q: And the gracious goddess, I ween, inclined her heart to pious sacrifices; and favourable signs appeared.

s: Jason’s spring is named for Jason (by the surrounding inhabitants)
q: the dwellers around in after times called that stream, the spring of Jason.

s: Heracles breaks Heracles’s broken oar (while rowing toward the Mysian mainland)
q: then Heracles, as he ploughed up the furrows of the roughened surge, broke his oar in the middle.

s: Heracles’s broken oar is broken Heracles (in the roughened surge)
q: then Heracles, as he ploughed up the furrows of the roughened surge, broke his oar in the middle.

s: Earthborn has six mighty hands (each individual)
q: for each one has six mighty hands to lift up, two from his sturdy shoulders, and four below, fitting close to his terrible sides.

s: Doliones dwells around isthmus (with their dwelling about the isthmus and plain)
q: And about the isthmus and the plain the Doliones had their dwelling

s: Doliones is protected by Poseidon (from the Earthborn)
q: But these men the Earthborn monsters, fearful though they were, in nowise harried, owing to the protection of Poseidon

s: Doliones descends from Poseidon (their first ancestor)
q: for from him had the Doliones first sprung.

s: Hylas is nurtured by Heracles (from childhood)
q: For in such ways did Heracles nurture him from his first childhood

s: Hylas is abducted by the water-nymph (at the spring Pegae)
q: and plunged him into the midst of the eddy.

s: Hylas becomes husband of the water-nymph (through her love for him)
q: But a goddess-nymph through love has made Hylas her husband

s: Hylas possesses Hylas’s bronze pitcher
q: Meantime Hylas with pitcher of bronze in hand had gone apart from the throng

s: Jason is a son of Aeson
q: And Aeson’s son, bewildered by their hapless plight, said never a word, good or bad

s: Jason is challenged by Telamon (over the abandonment of Heracles)
q: Sit there at thy ease, for it was fitting for thee to leave Heracles behind

s: Polyphemus is a hero
q: the hero Polyphemus, son of Eilatus

s: Polyphemus is destined to found Cius (at the mouth of the Cius among the Mysians)
q: Likewise it is destined for Polyphemus to found a glorious city at the mouth of Cius among the Mysians

s: Telamon is a son of Aeacus
q: Telamon son of Aeacus came in haste to Jason

s: Heracles is a son of Zeus
q: But the son of Zeus having duly enjoined on his comrades to prepare the feast took his way into a wood

s: Tiphys is a son of Hagnias
q: Tiphys son of Hagnias

s: Zeus determines Polyphemus’s founding of Cius (by divine counsel)
q: But of those two, by the counsel of Zeus, one, Polyphemus son of Eilatus, was destined to found and build a city among the Mysians bearing the river’s name

s: Phoebus is a Apollo (worshipped by the heroes before their feast)
q: after sacrificing at nightfall to Apollo Ecbasius.

s: Cypris causes the water-nymph’s love for Hylas (by making her heart faint)
q: And Cypris made her heart faint, and in her confusion she could scarcely gather her spirit back to her.

s: Heracles nurtures Hylas (from childhood)
q: For in such ways did Heracles nurture him from his first childhood

s: sons of Boreas are sons of Boreas (Thracian)
q: had not the two sons of Thracian Boreas held back the son of Aeacus with harsh words.

s: Minyan heroes are hospitably received by Mysians (in the Cianian land)
q: Them as they came in friendliness, the Mysians, inhabitants of that land, hospitably welcomed, and gave them in their need provisions and sheep and abundant wine.

s: Pegae is a spring (sacred and fair-flowing)
q: And quickly Hylas came to the spring which the people who dwell thereabouts call Pegae.

s: the water-nymph is a water-nymph (haunting the spring Pegae)
q: but one, a water-nymph was just rising from the fair-flowing spring

s: the water-nymph abducts Hylas (from the spring by plunging him into the eddy)
q: straightway she laid her left arm above upon his neck yearning to kiss his tender mouth; and with her right hand she drew down his elbow, and plunged him into the midst of the eddy.

s: Argo urges them (to go aboard and avail themselves of the wind)
q: and quickly did Tiphys urge them to go aboard and avail themselves of the wind.

s: Heracles kills Theiodamas (because he withstood him about an ox for the plough)
q: when he had carried him off from the house of his father, goodly Theiodamas, whom the hero pitilessly slew among the Dryopians because he withstood him about an ox for the plough.

s: the Argonauts’ abandonment of Heracles and Hylas causes a quarrel among the heroes (violent)
q: And a fierce quarrel fell upon them, and violent tumult, for that they had sailed and left behind the bravest of their comrades.

s: Heracles’ labors for Eurystheus number twelve (destined at Argos)
q: At Argos it is his fate to labour for insolent Eurystheus and to accomplish full twelve toils

s: the pledges and oath concerning the search for Hylas are given by Mysians (the noblest sons serving as pledges)
q: And for him they gave pledges choosing out the noblest sons of the people and took an oath that they would never cease from their labour of search.

s: Heracles labors for Eurystheus (by fate at Argos)
q: At Argos it is his fate to labour for insolent Eurystheus and to accomplish full twelve toils

s: Heracles dwells with the immortals (after fulfilling his labors)
q: and dwell with the immortals, if so be that he bring to fulfilment a few more yet

s: Heracles possesses Heracles’ bronze-tipped club
q: and took off his lion’s skin. And he loosened the pine from the ground with his bronze-tipped club

s: Heracles threatens Mysians (with laying waste their land if Hylas’s fate is not discovered)
q: And he threatened to lay waste the Mysian land at once, should they not discover for him the doom of Hylas, whether living or dead.

s: Hylas is a son of Theiodamas
q: Hylas the son of Theiodamas

s: Amycus is a king (of the Bebrycians)
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Bebrycians is a people (ruled by Amycus)
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Bebrycians inhabit Bebrycia
q: so they stayed steadfast no longer, but scattered themselves inland through Bebrycia, proclaiming the death of Amycus

s: Bebrycians are ruled by Amycus (as king)
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Bebrycians attacks Polydeuces (with rough clubs and spears)
q: Nor were the Bebrycians reckless of their king; but all together took up rough clubs and spears and rushed straight on Polydeuces.

s: Bebrycia contains Amycus's farm and oxstalls
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Polydeuces is a Argonaut hero (champion of his comrades)
q: And quickly he stood forth his comrades’ champion, and cried:

s: Polydeuces is son of Tyndareus
q: Hereupon the son of Tyndareus laid aside his mantle

s: Polydeuces is son of Zeus (divine parentage)
q: Such was the son of Zeus, the bloom of the first down still on his cheeks, still with the look of gladness in his eyes.

s: Polydeuces is skilled in boxing (defeating Amycus)
q: for we will obey thy rules, as thou sayest. Willingly now do I myself undertake to meet thee.

s: Amycus is son of Poseidon
q: whom once a nymph, Bithynian Melie, united to Poseidon Genethlius, bare the most arrogant of men

s: Polydeuces kills Amycus (in a boxing contest)
q: with a rush he struck him above the ear, and broke the bones inside, and the king in agony fell upon his knees; and the Minyan heroes shouted for joy; and his life was poured forth all at once.

s: Polydeuces is celebrated by song celebrating Polydeuces (as the Therapnaean son of Zeus)
q: and they celebrated the Therapnaean son of Zeus.[14]

s: Minyan heroes drives off their countless sheep (from all sides)
q: And now the foe was destroying their steadings and farms, and now the heroes from all sides were driving off their countless sheep

s: Minyan heroes defeat Bebrycians (after Polydeuces kills Amycus)
q: so the heroes grievously scared the arrogant Bebrycians

s: Minyan heroes has placed at their feet two pairs of gauntlets (made of raw hide)
q: And between them Lyeoreus, the henchman of Amycus, placed at their feet on each side two pairs of gauntlets made of raw hide, dry, exceeding tough.

s: Argo is steered by Tiphys (through the Bosporus storm)
q: So they by the steering-craft of Tiphys escaped, unhurt but sore dismayed.

s: Amycus's boxing challenge requires strangers (Bebrycia) (to box before departing)
q: It is the rule that no stranger who comes to the Bebrycians should depart till he has raised his hands in battle against mine.

s: Amycus is son of Bithynian Melie (through her union with Poseidon Genethlius)
q: whom once a nymph, Bithynian Melie, united to Poseidon Genethlius, bare the most arrogant of men

s: the Bosporus storm is a dangerous sea wave (encountered by the Argonauts’ ship)
q: Hereupon a wave like a steep mountain rose aloft in front as though rushing upon them

s: the Bosporus storm is survived by Argo (through Tiphys’s steering)
q: So they by the steering-craft of Tiphys escaped, unhurt but sore dismayed.

s: Tiphys is a helmsman (of the Argonauts’ ship)
q: So they by the steering-craft of Tiphys escaped, unhurt but sore dismayed.

s: Tiphys steers Argo (through the Bosporus storm)
q: So they by the steering-craft of Tiphys escaped, unhurt but sore dismayed.

s: Bosporus contains the Bosporus storm (on the heroes’ route)
q: with a favouring wind they steered through the eddying Bosporus. Hereupon a wave like a steep mountain rose aloft in front

s: Amycus is arrogant most arrogant of men
q: whom once a nymph, Bithynian Melie, united to Poseidon Genethlius, bare the most arrogant of men

s: Amycus rules Bebrycians (as king)
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Amycus possesses Amycus's farm and oxstalls (in Bebrycia)
q: Here were the oxstalls and farm of Amycus, the haughty king of the Bebrycians

s: Amycus imposes Amycus's boxing challenge (on strangers who enter Bebrycia)
q: for even for strangers he laid down an insulting ordinance, that none should depart till they had made trial of him in boxing

s: Amycus is killed in Amycus’s boxing match and death (after being struck above the ear by Polydeuces)
q: and coming near and slipping his knee past the king’s, with a rush he struck him above the ear, and broke the bones inside, and the king in agony fell upon his knees; and the Minyan heroes shouted for joy; and his life was poured forth all at once.

s: Phineus is a son of Agenor
q: There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea

s: Phineus is helped by sons of Boreas (they restrain the Harpies)
q: These pests, the oracle declares, the sons of Boreas shall restrain.
